questions.question: What are Angular lifecycle hooks? Explain ngOnInit, ngOnChanges, ngAfterViewInit and ngOnDestroy.

definition.text: Lifecycle hooks run code at defined component lifetime stages.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Angular creates components, supplies inputs, checks templates, renders views and eventually tears instances down. The framework offers hooks so component code can react to those distinct stages instead of guessing when inputs, queries or cleanup opportunities are available.
motivation.historicalNote: The commonly taught class lifecycle includes ngOnChanges, ngOnInit, ngAfterViewInit and ngOnDestroy. Modern Angular also provides render callbacks such as afterNextRender and DestroyRef for cleanup. ngOnChanges can also observe signal inputs.

problemSolved.before: Code in a constructor may read inputs too early, and intervals or subscriptions can outlive destroyed views.
problemSolved.after: Choose hooks based on timing: ngOnChanges reacts to bound input changes, ngOnInit runs once after initialization, ngAfterViewInit runs once after view initialization, and ngOnDestroy handles teardown.
benefits: Input changes can trigger a documented callback
View query readiness has a defined boundary

characteristics: ngOnChanges runs for bound input changes, including the initial assignment; initial invocation precedes ngOnInit
ngOnInit runs once after component inputs receive their initial values
ngAfterViewInit runs once after the component view is initialized; changing checked state there can cause an error
ngOnDestroy runs once before the component instance is destroyed
DestroyRef and takeUntilDestroyed offer composable cleanup; afterNextRender is better for some browser DOM work

simpleAnalogy.title: Theater performance schedule
simpleAnalogy.explanation: The theater has setup, rehearsal, curtain-up and teardown stages. A technician cannot inspect the finished stage before setup, and lights must be switched off after the show; hooks provide analogous timing boundaries.

industryExample.scenario: A shipment detail view receives a shipment ID, renders a tracking timeline and optionally starts a status refresh while visible.
industryExample.implementation: Accept the shipment ID as an input; react to a changed ID; initialize view data; query view-only UI after it exists; stop a timer during teardown. Prefer declarative streams and lifecycle-safe cleanup over manual timers for production.
industryExample.businessImpact: Correct shipment is displayed after navigation and stale polling does not continue after leaving the page.
industryExample.importantConstraint: Client teardown does not cancel server-side business processing. Keep subscription lifetimes explicit; SSR environments may not have browser DOM APIs.

useCases: Initialize a form from resolved inputs
Respond to a parent changing an input
Access a view query once the view has initialized
Stop a repeating client-side task on destruction
Integrate third-party visualization with browser rendering lifecycle

steps: Parent creates shipment detail component
Angular binds shipmentId from parent
ngOnChanges receives initial shipmentId change
ngOnInit runs once after initial inputs are initialized
Angular creates and initializes the component view
ngAfterViewInit can inspect the view child
Parent changes shipmentId and ngOnChanges runs again
Navigation destroys the component; ngOnDestroy clears its timer

diagrams.title: Component lifecycle hooks: lifecycle and industry flow
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Parent
    participant A as Angular
    participant C as ShipmentDetail
    participant T as Timer
    P->>A: Bind shipmentId
    A->>C: ngOnChanges initial ID
    A->>C: ngOnInit once
    A->>C: ngAfterViewInit once
    C->>T: Start optional refresh timer
    P->>A: Change shipmentId
    A->>C: ngOnChanges updated ID
    A->>C: ngOnDestroy on navigation
    C->>T: Clear interval
diagrams.caption: The diagram simplifies template checking; actual hooks run as part of Angular change detection and view lifecycle.

codeExample.runtime: Angular 20+ compatible standalone component; place in an Angular CLI project; no external HTML required
explanation: Decorator-based @Input is used deliberately to make ngOnChanges timing visible
Initial ngOnChanges runs before ngOnInit; ngAfterViewInit runs after the view initializes
The interval updates a Signal so even zoneless change detection observes the UI change; a real app should use deliberate polling/data strategies
ngOnDestroy removes the interval to avoid work continuing after navigation
Direct DOM access should be limited and guarded for non-browser rendering

projectExperience.example: In the logistics learning portal, I would build shipment detail screens whose refresh work stops when the route changes, then show a test that demonstrates correct teardown.
evidenceToCollect: Test fixture records of hook execution order
Browser navigation recording that the timer stops
projectExperience.doNotClaim: This is a proposed training-project implementation; do not claim that it was deployed or delivered to real customers.

pitfalls: ngAfterViewInit is not a general-purpose place to mutate bound state; it may cause ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError
ngOnChanges reacts to input bindings, not arbitrary mutations of fields elsewhere
ngOnDestroy is skipped if the entire browser process is abruptly killed; server cleanup is separate
Manual subscriptions and intervals left running after destroy cause leaks
Assuming browser DOM availability during SSR breaks server rendering
whenNotToUse: Do not use ngOnInit to detect every later input change
Do not introduce lifecycle hooks when computed signals/template bindings express the behavior more simply
Do not manipulate elements in the constructor or use ngAfterViewInit for unguarded server-side DOM access

alternatives.name: computed() on signal inputs
alternatives.bestFor: Deriving a value from a changing input without side effects
alternatives.tradeoff: Not a replacement for teardown or imperative integration

alternatives.name: DestroyRef/onDestroy
alternatives.bestFor: Co-locating resource cleanup with resource creation

alternatives.name: afterNextRender
alternatives.bestFor: Performing browser DOM work after Angular renders
alternatives.tradeoff: Does not run in SSR and must be called in an injection context

testing.strategy: Use Angular TestBed and component fixtures for isolated behavior; combine with browser checks for UI interactions.

testCases.expected: ngOnChanges initial record occurs before ngOnInit and ngAfterViewInit
ngOnChanges receives a new value but ngOnInit does not rerun
Interval is cleared when fixture.destroy() is called

negativeCases: Mutating state synchronously inside ngAfterViewInit may trigger expression-changed errors
A missing @Input binding with required input should produce a template compile error
Destroy and recreate should not leave multiple timers alive

intermediate: How does takeUntilDestroyed differ from manually subscribing?
advanced: How would SSR change render-time DOM integration?
expert: How would you instrument lifecycle-related resource leaks across hundreds of routed screens?

answer.finalTakeaway: Choose hooks by lifecycle timing, but prefer declarative state and automatic cleanup when possible.

learningOutcomes: Explain initialization, change, view and destruction phases
Predict first and later ngOnChanges behavior
Show a lifecycle-safe resource cleanup pattern

questions.question: What is the difference between the constructor and ngOnInit()?

definition.text: Constructors initialize instances; ngOnInit runs after input initialization.

motivation.whyIntroduced: TypeScript constructors are part of class creation; Angular-specific startup must occur after Angular has assigned inputs. Separating these steps avoids reading unavailable input values while constructing an instance.
motivation.historicalNote: The class constructor is JavaScript/TypeScript syntax, not an Angular lifecycle hook. ngOnInit is called by Angular once after inputs have their initial values. Modern field initializers may use inject() within injection context.

problemSolved.before: An API call started in the constructor may use a default empty ID because the parent has not yet bound the actual account ID.
problemSolved.after: Use the constructor for minimal instance setup; initialize work that depends on an initial input during ngOnInit or use input-based reactive derivation.

characteristics: Constructor executes whenever a component class instance is constructed
Angular calls ngOnInit once per component instance
Initial input values are available to ngOnInit, but are not guaranteed in the constructor
Neither constructor nor ngOnInit waits for asynchronous HTTP requests
A changing input does not automatically rerun ngOnInit

simpleAnalogy.title: Restaurant seating and first order
simpleAnalogy.explanation: Building a table sets up chairs and menus (constructor). Only after diners arrive can the waiter read their order (initial input / ngOnInit).

industryExample.scenario: A parent account page passes a current account ID into a transaction summary.
industryExample.implementation: Declare @Input accountId with a required binding. Initialize an account-specific label in ngOnInit rather than the constructor; if account IDs can change later, react via ngOnChanges or signal-based computed state.
industryExample.businessImpact: The first transaction summary references the account chosen by the parent, not a temporary default.
industryExample.importantConstraint: Fetching confidential account data requires backend account authorization regardless of which hook initiates the request.

useCases: Reading a required initial input
Setting up a component-specific initial view model
Initializing a form once from initial input data
Explaining dependency injection availability during class construction
Preventing early access to view children

steps: Angular constructs an AccountSummary instance
Constructor executes with default field values
Angular assigns bound accountId
Angular calls ngOnChanges for the initial bound value when implemented
Angular calls ngOnInit
Component displays the correct initialized label

diagrams.title: Constructor versus ngOnInit: lifecycle and industry flow
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Parent
    participant A as Angular
    participant C as AccountSummary
    A->>C: new AccountSummary()
    C-->>A: constructor completes
    P->>A: Bind accountId = ACC-42
    A->>C: Assign bound input
    A->>C: ngOnChanges (if implemented)
    A->>C: ngOnInit once
    C-->>P: Render account summary
diagrams.caption: Angular input assignment occurs after construction and before ngOnInit; the sequence represents the initial lifecycle only.

codeExample.runtime: Angular 20+ compatible standalone component; place in an Angular CLI project
explanation: The constructor runs during ordinary class instantiation
@Input is assigned by Angular after construction
ngOnInit uses the initial parent-provided accountId
The label will not recompute on later input changes; handle those separately
For a purely derived label in modern Angular, signal input() + computed() is often better

projectExperience.example: For a banking training app, I would use initial input values to set up an account detail view and use computed signals if the selected account can change while the component remains mounted.
evidenceToCollect: Screenshot showing correct account ID after initial binding
Regression test for changing IDs, followed by a computed-input improvement
projectExperience.doNotClaim: This is a proposed training-project implementation; do not claim that it was deployed or delivered to real customers.

pitfalls: Expecting a bound @Input value to be available in the constructor
Putting work into ngOnInit and assuming it runs on every parameter update
Starting asynchronous work without error/cancellation handling
Performing expensive operations in the constructor slows component creation
Treating input-based initialization as authorization
whenNotToUse: Do not fetch input-dependent data using an uninitialized constructor input
Do not put unconditional network calls in constructors merely because the constructor runs first
Do not use ngOnInit for a derived value that must update whenever its source input changes

alternatives.name: input() + computed()
alternatives.bestFor: Pure values derived from parent inputs across updates

alternatives.name: ngOnChanges
alternatives.bestFor: Imperative reactions to later input changes

alternatives.name: RxJS switchMap
alternatives.bestFor: Cancel stale API requests when input IDs change
alternatives.tradeoff: Requires an observable input source and deliberate error handling

testing.strategy: Use Angular TestBed and component fixtures for isolated behavior; combine with browser checks for UI interactions.

testCases.expected: Rendered label matches the bound accountId
Constructor log shows default value rather than assuming the parent value
Demonstrate that ngOnInit does not rerun; a reactive alternative updates if implemented

negativeCases: Without a required accountId binding, modern Angular template compilation should reject the usage
Reusing an existing instance with a different bound accountId leaves the sample label unchanged

intermediate: How do you handle a required input changing after init?
advanced: How would you cancel an account request when route inputs change quickly?
expert: When would a signal-derived view model be preferable to hook-driven mutable state?

answer.finalTakeaway: Constructors create objects; input-aware setup belongs after Angular supplies initial inputs.

learningOutcomes: Distinguish class construction from Angular lifecycle
Predict input availability for both phases
Identify cases where reactive derivation is better than ngOnInit

questions.question: How does parent-to-child and child-to-parent component communication work?

definition.text: Inputs send data downward; outputs communicate events upward.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Component trees need a predictable, explicit way to exchange values without children reaching directly into parent internals. Angular inputs declare inbound data contracts; outputs declare notifications that the parent handles.
motivation.historicalNote: Modern Angular prefers signal-based input() for many new components and output() for custom events. Existing apps also use @Input(), @Output() and EventEmitter. Output events do not automatically bubble through DOM ancestors.

problemSolved.before: A child reaching into a parent singleton or mutating a shared object can accidentally change unrelated screens and obscure who owns state.
problemSolved.after: A parent binds data into a child input; the child emits an event describing user intent; the parent decides how to update its state.
benefits: Explicit contracts between parent and child

characteristics: Inputs define a public inbound API
Outputs define an event API
The parent normally owns state passed down
Typed values improve template checking
Events are notifications, not backend authorization

simpleAnalogy.title: TV remote and television
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A television receives a selected channel (input). The remote sends a change request (event) and the owning controller decides the next channel; the remote does not rewrite the television hardware.

industryExample.scenario: A product-list page shows product cards and handles Add to cart clicks.
industryExample.implementation: Pass a typed Product into each product-card input and emit productId when Add to cart is clicked. The parent updates cart state and may later call a backend API.
industryExample.businessImpact: Product cards remain reusable across catalog and recommendations, while cart mutations are coordinated in one place.
industryExample.importantConstraint: A frontend Add to cart event is not a confirmed order; price, stock and permissions must be revalidated on the backend at checkout.

useCases: Reusable product-card buttons
Filter components notifying a results page
Modal confirmation events
Editable row controls that send save requests upward
Wizard steps receiving form state from a parent

steps: Parent owns a Product and cart array
Parent binds Product into product-card input
Child renders title and price
User activates Add to cart
Child emits product ID via output()
Parent handles event and updates cart state
Angular updates displayed cart count

diagrams.title: Parent-child communication: lifecycle and industry flow
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    actor U as Shopper
    participant P as CatalogPage
    participant C as ProductCard
    U->>P: Open catalog
    P->>C: [product] = selected product
    C-->>U: Render product details
    U->>C: Click Add to cart
    C->>P: addToCart.emit(productId)
    P->>P: Update cart signal
    P-->>U: Show updated cart count
diagrams.caption: Output emits a component event handled by its immediate binding consumer; Angular custom outputs do not bubble like DOM click events.

codeExample.runtime: Angular 20+ standalone components; input()/output() stable modern Angular APIs
explanation: input.required<Product>() expresses the required inbound product contract
output<string>() emits an ID, not a mutable shared product object
The parent owns the cartIds signal and updates it when the child emits
Signals update the cart count in the template
This represents client-side cart intent; persisted cart operations need APIs and business rules

projectExperience.example: In the e-commerce learning project I would keep product-card components presentation-focused and make the catalog page or a dedicated cart feature responsible for mutations.
evidenceToCollect: Component test proving the product name renders
Component test proving button emits the correct product ID
Parent test showing exactly one item is added per click
projectExperience.doNotClaim: This is a proposed training-project implementation; do not claim that it was deployed or delivered to real customers.

pitfalls: Mutating an input object in the child can bypass clear ownership boundaries
Outputs do not bubble automatically through arbitrary ancestor components
Naming an output click or another native DOM event can be confusing
Events can be emitted more than once if buttons are not disabled during processing
Passing large shared mutable objects makes change tracking and tests less predictable
whenNotToUse: Do not use outputs for unrelated components separated by many layers when a service or state store fits better
Do not treat child events as proof that an order succeeded
Do not require a child to know its parent component class just to communicate

alternatives.name: Shared feature service
alternatives.bestFor: Multiple sibling or distant components that share state
alternatives.tradeoff: Requires carefully scoped ownership and teardown

alternatives.name: model() input
alternatives.bestFor: Reusable controls with explicit two-way binding contracts
alternatives.tradeoff: May obscure ownership if used for every field

alternatives.name: Router or URL state
alternatives.bestFor: State that should survive navigation or be shareable
alternatives.tradeoff: Not suited to ephemeral button events

testing.strategy: Use Angular TestBed and component fixtures for isolated behavior; combine with browser checks for UI interactions.

testCases.expected: Product name appears from bound parent input
Click emits SKU-1 and parent cart count becomes one
Cart count follows expected business logic for duplicates

negativeCases: Omitting required product input should cause a template compilation diagnostic
A handler that adds twice per click reveals duplicate subscriptions or bindings
Changing a product input should update the card without rebuilding the entire page

advanced: How do Signals affect input change detection and event handling?
expert: How would you design shared cart state across lazy-loaded modules without duplicate updates?

answer.finalTakeaway: Data flows down through inputs; user intent flows up through typed outputs.

learningOutcomes: Distinguish UI intent events from successful backend actions

questions.topic: Inputs and outputs versus shared services
questions.question: What are the differences between input/output bindings and sharing data through a service?

definition.text: Inputs and outputs connect relatives; services coordinate shared state.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Passing inputs across several intermediate components creates prop drilling, while unrelated components may need the same authenticated session or filter state. A service offers a shared, injectable owner where direct communication is awkward.
motivation.historicalNote: Angular has long supported hierarchical DI and component bindings. Modern Signals make small scoped state services straightforward, but the service provider scope determines whether state is shared or duplicated.

problemSolved.before: A header, sidebar and account screen each manage a separate selected-account value and drift out of sync.
problemSolved.after: Use input/output for local parent-child contracts; use a correctly scoped state service for cross-tree shared state, while keeping server state and authorization boundaries explicit.

characteristics: Inputs/outputs keep ownership visible for immediate relatives
Services are injected via hierarchical providers
A root provider can share state across an application
Component-level providers create isolated service instances
Signals can expose readonly state and explicit mutation methods

simpleAnalogy.title: Passing notes versus shared notice board
simpleAnalogy.explanation: Two people sitting together can pass a note directly. Several teams in different rooms may need a shared notice board managed by an owner; everyone sees the same announcement.

industryExample.scenario: An enterprise workspace selector appears in a global header while the project list and permissions summary appear in separate feature areas.
industryExample.implementation: A WorkspaceContextService stores the active workspace identifier as a private signal and exposes a readonly value. Header changes it; workspace-filtered screens read it and reload their authorized data.
industryExample.businessImpact: Cross-feature navigation stays consistent when the user changes workspaces.
industryExample.importantConstraint: The browser service is not an isolation boundary. Backend APIs must validate workspace membership on every request and clear/cache-key workspace-specific data appropriately.

useCases: Authentication session summary in header and settings
Active tenant or workspace context
Cross-feature notification state
Shared shopping-cart badge across routes
Synchronized feature-level filters

steps: Angular root injector creates one WorkspaceContextService instance for the application root
Header injects service and calls selectWorkspace
Private writable signal receives new workspace ID
Other consumers read readonly currentWorkspace signal
UI updates to show chosen workspace
Data clients refetch or invalidate cache using the new workspace context
Backend checks the user belongs to that workspace

diagrams.title: Inputs and outputs versus shared services: lifecycle and industry flow
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[Workspace Header] -->|selectWorkspace| B[WorkspaceContextService]
  B --> C[Private activeWorkspace signal]
  C --> D[Readonly workspace view]
  D --> E[Project List]
  D --> F[Permissions Summary]
  E --> G[Workspace aware API]
  F --> G
  G --> H[Backend authorization]
diagrams.caption: The service shares browser-side selection only; backend verification remains mandatory and API fetching is intentionally not implemented in this short example.

explanation: Root-provided service shares one instance in the application environment injector
The writable signal stays private; consumers receive a readonly signal
Header performs an explicit state transition rather than mutating the value
A separate status component observes changes automatically
Root singleton does not persist across browser reloads, tabs, or server render requests

projectExperience.example: In a SaaS training portal I would use parent-child bindings for isolated user-row actions and a workspace context service for the active workspace across feature routes.
evidenceToCollect: Test demonstrating header and status share one root service instance
Test proving a component-scoped override produces isolated state
Security test showing unauthorized workspace APIs are rejected
projectExperience.doNotClaim: This is a proposed training-project implementation; do not claim that it was deployed or delivered to real customers.

pitfalls: Providing the same state service on multiple feature components can create unexpected separate instances
Global root services can retain stale sensitive information across sign-out
Readonly signal prevents direct writes but does not provide deep immutable object protection
Shared services can grow into unmaintainable god-objects
Browser state is not shared across tabs or persisted without an explicit strategy
whenNotToUse: Do not introduce a root singleton for an isolated one-child interaction
Do not rely on a client service to enforce tenant boundaries
Do not make one service responsible for unrelated features merely to avoid passing inputs

alternatives.name: input/output
alternatives.bestFor: Direct parent-child data and intent exchange
alternatives.tradeoff: Can require forwarding across many levels

alternatives.name: Component-scoped service
alternatives.bestFor: State shared only within one feature subtree
alternatives.tradeoff: Consumers outside the subtree cannot see that instance

alternatives.name: Central state library
alternatives.bestFor: Complex cross-feature state with devtools and standardized effects

testing.strategy: Use Angular TestBed and component fixtures for isolated behavior; combine with browser checks for UI interactions.

testCases.expected: Click header button and verify status shows demo-workspace
Override provider at a test host and verify another subtree remains independent
Clearing workspace on sign-out removes stale UI context

negativeCases: A child provider shadows root service unexpectedly
Opening another tab does not automatically update state
Reading a stale workspace during an in-flight API response requires cancellation or guarded rendering

intermediate: How does provider hierarchy affect service instance scope?
advanced: How would you prevent cross-tenant cache leakage after workspace switching?
expert: How should a multi-tenant front end coordinate state across SSR, browser tabs and server-side authorization?

answer.finalTakeaway: Use direct bindings for local contracts and scoped services for genuinely shared state.

learningOutcomes: Choose a communication approach based on component relationship
Explain provider scope and instance duplication
Name the server-side safeguards for tenant-aware state

questions.question: Build a parent component that passes account data to a child and receives a button-click event from that child.

definition.text: Parent supplies typed account data; child emits selection events.

motivation.whyIntroduced: A realistic UI must reuse account presentation while keeping navigation decisions and permissions outside the card. Inputs express the card data contract; output events let the containing screen react to selection without coupling the card to routing.
motivation.historicalNote: The recommended modern implementation uses input.required<T>() and output<T>(). @Input and @Output remain relevant for reading existing Angular applications. output() events are not DOM-bubbling events.

problemSolved.before: A duplicated account card hardcodes navigation and reads a global service directly; the same card becomes difficult to reuse for search results and overview screens.
problemSolved.after: A typed child accepts readonly account information and emits a selected ID; its parent owns the selection state and determines the next UI action.

characteristics: Required input provides a typed component contract
Output emits a meaningful event payload
Parent owns the selected account state
Child exposes no backend authorization logic
Accessible button supports keyboard activation

simpleAnalogy.title: Library book card
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A library shelf gives each book card its title and ID. When someone selects a card, it reports the book ID to the library desk, which decides what to open next.

industryExample.scenario: A banking dashboard shows two fictional accounts and lets the customer select one for a detail panel.
industryExample.implementation: Create an AccountCard component with input.required<AccountSummary>() and output<string>(). The dashboard renders cards using @for with stable account IDs and updates its own selectedId signal on output.
industryExample.businessImpact: One reusable card handles multiple account types and a parent owns selection decisions; switching accounts updates the panel predictably.
industryExample.importantConstraint: The example uses illustrative minor-unit balances only. Never authorize account access or financial transfers based on a client-supplied ID alone.

useCases: Dashboard account cards
Selectable patient records in administrative lists
Product selection from search results
Shipment list to detail navigation
Workspace overview cards

steps: Dashboard owns an array of typed account summaries
@for renders AccountCard for each summary using account ID as tracking key
Angular binds each account to the child input
User activates View details
Child emits selected account ID
Dashboard handles selected event and updates signal
Selected-account label updates; a real detail API would verify permission

The card output sends the ID without changing parent data

An output event may be emitted more than once by repeated clicks; enforce idempotency in real workflows
Displaying real account numbers or raw sensitive IDs can expose private data
Using a floating-point number as a source of truth for money is unsafe
whenNotToUse: Do not call the payments backend directly from a generic display card
Do not put tenant or account authorization in the child component
Do not store secret account data in browser code or checked-in JSON
Do not use a two-way model binding merely to report a button click

alternatives.tradeoff: Too much coupling for a one-way selection event

alternatives.name: Shared service
alternatives.tradeoff: Adds scope and consistency concerns absent in a simple parent-child pattern
